title: Twenty-two machines in one week

summary.text: <u>Twenty-two machines joined the floor in a single week</u>, taking the collection to 61 machines, 57 of them open to visitors. Three Xerox machines arrived together: the *1973* [Alto II](station:alto), where the desktop and the mouse began; the *1981* [Star 8010](station:star) *"Dandelion"* running **ViewPoint 2.0**; and the *1985* [Xerox 6085](station:daybreak) *"Daybreak"*. DEC is here as three different PDP-11s now — **2.11BSD** on a [PDP-11/70](station:pdp11), the oldest lineage in the collection; the *1973* [GT40](station:gt40), a small one wired to a vector display and a light pen, drawing **Lunar Lander**; and a third [PDP-11](station:decos) that lets you pick **RT-11**, **RSX-11M** or **RSTS/E** at the prompt. Seven home computers came in one wave, from the [ZX Spectrum](station:zxspectrum) to the [BBC Micro](station:bbcmicro) and the *68008* [Sinclair QL](station:sinclairql), joined by four more Commodores, a *NeXTcube* running [NeXTSTEP 3.3](station:nextstep), a second [SGI Indy](station:indyr4400), and the [ARM Evaluation System](station:armeval) — the first ARM product ever sold. Two *AlphaServer*s closed the week: [Windows 2000 RC2](station:w2kalpha), the last Windows ever built for *Alpha*, and [Tru64 UNIX 5.1B](station:tru64).

Every machine is now shown as its own screen and nothing else: the emulator's window furniture is out of the picture entirely. The [Alto](station:alto) is the proof. It stands up, in the tall portrait shape of its own display — 606 by 808 dots, the proportions of a sheet of paper — with no letterbox and nothing painted around it. A few machines never had a pointer that could jump straight to where you touch; their cursor drifts toward it instead, and those now say so before you open one, so period behaviour does not read as a fault. And the [ARM Evaluation System](station:armeval), which has no operating system to type into, puts its four commands on screen at one tap each.

Machines used to boot when you opened them. Now they are simply left running, held at the moment they were last used, and wake in well under a second — no boot sequence you did not ask to watch. [Windows 2000 on the *Alpha*](station:w2kalpha) picks up exactly where it stopped, its own clock included, and answers in ten seconds where it used to take twenty-five. Pointing at [NeXTSTEP](station:nextstep) finally works the way you expect: the cursor lands where you put it. And typing got honest — hammer a line into the [KC 85/4](station:kc854) or the [Micro-Professor](station:mpf2) and every letter arrives, in order, so "HELLO" no longer turns up as "HLLO".

bullets: The [PET 2001](station:pet2001) of *1977*: screen, keyboard and cassette deck welded into one sheet-metal trapezoid you could carry home and switch on
The [CBM 8032](station:cbm8032) is Commodore's office machine — 80 columns of green text, and no colour, no sprites and no sound chip at all
The [C128](station:c128) is three computers in one case, and the only machine here that can show you **CP/M**, the office system MS-DOS replaced
The [CBM 610](station:cbm2) says 128 on the screen and is not a C128: Commodore's *1982* try at a business computer, cancelled almost immediately
The [ZX81](station:zx81): £69.95 in kit form, one kilobyte of memory, no sound and no colour — and a million and a half of them sold
The [Oric Atmos](station:oricatmos) has a BASIC in which ZAP, PING, SHOOT and EXPLODE each make the noise they are named after
The Welsh-built [Dragon 32](station:dragon32) runs a *Motorola 6809*, the best *8-bit* processor anyone shipped, and cannot draw a lower-case letter
The [KC 85/4](station:kc854) was East Germany's school computer, and it prints its own list of commands at power-on so a beginner has somewhere to start
Each of the [ZX Spectrum](station:zxspectrum)'s forty rubber keys carries a whole BASIC word: press P and PRINT appears
The [Sinclair QL](station:sinclairql) shipped with firmware that did not fit — the earliest buyers got the missing part on a cartridge hanging out of the back
The [BBC Micro](station:bbcmicro)'s BASIC has a *6502* assembler inside it, and the team who finished the machine went on to design the *ARM*
Reaching the [Star](station:star)'s desktop once meant a 22-minute cold boot and six keystrokes; it is now sitting there waiting when you arrive
Every window on the [6085](station:daybreak) has a named tab instead of a title bar, and a line of prose along the top narrates what the system is doing
The [GT40](station:gt40) has no pixels at all — an electron beam draws each line exactly where the program says, and nothing in between
The two [SGI Indys](station:indyr4400) sit side by side on purpose: same blue case, same **IRIX 6.5**, a different *MIPS* chip inside each
[Tru64](station:tru64) was born *OSF/1* in 1992 and ended with 5.1B in 2003, when HP retired it and *Alpha* together
Three operating systems on one [PDP-11](station:decos), because in 1975 you bought a computer and then chose one to run on it
Log into the [PDP-11/70](station:pdp11) as root — there is no password — and the whole operating system's source code is sitting in /usr/src
